https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/ai-startu.title: AI startup Numa raises $45 million to help car dealerships leave the paperwork behind
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/ai-startu.author: Camila Grigera Naón
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence promises to untangle the messy workflows that have long plagued legacy industries. One startup is bringing that pitch to car dealerships. On Monday, Oakland-based company Numa announced a $45 million Series C round to build out an AI operating system designed to handle the daily grind of dealership customer service, from answering calls and booking appointments to keeping customers updated on their cars.

It works like this: Numa’s AI agents connect to a dealership’s software to check inventory down to a car’s trim and features, pull repair updates and log sales leads alongside conversation transcripts. The platform also handles routine warranty paperwork and flags exchanges that may signal an unhappy customer for managers to review.

“Think about things like filling out warranty paperwork. That is a drudgery of a job that nobody wants to do, and people do it poorly. You can apply an AI and do it instantly,” Numa CEO Tasso Roumeliotis told Fortune.

Blue Cloud Ventures led the round, bringing Numa’s total funding to $96 million. Threshold Ventures, Costanoa Ventures, Touring Capital, Gradient Ventures, Mitsui and Tokio Marine also participated. Founded in 2017, Numa previously raised seed and Series A funding from investors including Draper Fisher Jurvetson. The latest round valued Numa at $500 million after the investment, according to a source familiar with the company.

Numa’s pitch comes as more companies put AI agents to work. In a survey of roughly 2,100 senior leaders across 20 countries and industries ranging from automotive to healthcare, accounting and consulting firm KPMG found that 34% reported widespread employee adoption of AI agents in the third quarter of 2026, up from 25% in the first quarter.
For Roumeliotis, Numa began with a familiar team and a new problem to solve.

He had previously built Location Labs, a mobile technology company that tapped into the early spread of GPS-enabled cellphones to help people track one another’s locations. After selling the business in 2015, he joined venture firm Draper Fisher Jurvetson as an entrepreneur-in-residence.

While he was there, former colleagues from Location Labs approached him with a proposition: They wanted to build another company together. The group included engineers, product specialists and executives who had taken on bigger roles under Roumeliotis.

In 2017, they launched Number AI to help small businesses receive and respond to texts through their existing landline numbers, using natural language processing to bring newer technology to businesses still relying on older tools.

But as they worked with car dealerships, they found problems that went beyond missed messages. Employees juggled calls, paperwork and manual follow-ups, leaving customers waiting. The team narrowed its focus to the automotive industry and renamed the company Numa.
Blue Cloud Ventures also saw an opportunity in dealerships still relying on older software.

“I look at the auto dealership… as a little bit like jumbo shrimp. It’s a massive niche,” Mir Arif, the venture capital firm’s managing partner, told Fortune. “All of them [are still] working off legacy software or literally pen and paper.”

Today, the company has about 160 employees across its Bay Area headquarters, a sales and marketing office in Kansas City and an AI development office in Montreal. More than 1,500 dealerships in the U.S. and Canada use its software, including Longo Toyota, Norm Reeves Honda and Gold Coast Cadillac.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/arist-ceo.title: AI could soon be telling CEOs whom to lay off, Arist CEO Michael Ioffe predicts: ‘The speed of decision making is so much faster’
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/arist-ceo.author: Tatiana Sataua
paragraphs: AI is already fueling workers’ fears of being replaced. Now, one startup CEO predicts it could soon help companies decide whether to lay them off, too.

“We do expect that within the next few years, the majority of significant enterprise shifts, whether it’s products you’re launching, you know, layoffs that you’re making, et cetera, will be recommended by agents,” Michael Ioffe, cofounder and CEO of Arist, said while speaking with Fortune‘s Kristin Stoller at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit.

Ioffe’s company uses AI agents to interview employees, comb through company data, and recommend solutions to business problems. Arist already works with more than 15% of the Fortune 500, and its technology can gather insights from thousands of employees in just 72 hours—a process that traditionally requires teams of consultants. Still, he doesn’t envision executives handing over control entirely.
“At the end of the day, it will always be an executive who is making the final call,” Ioffe said.

That prediction comes as more companies cite AI when cutting jobs, sometimes drawing accusations of “AI washing,” or blaming technology for cuts made for other reasons. But even when companies genuinely expect AI to replace workers, moving too quickly can backfire. As Stoller previously reported, HR leaders have warned that companies risk losing valuable talent when they cut workers without a clear plan for how AI will replace their work.

For Ioffe, the appeal is speed. When sales fall or a product struggles, companies often spend months and millions of dollars working with consultants to understand why. He believes AI can help executives get answers in days rather than months.

Ioffe didn’t set out to compete with consulting firms. At 19, he became interested in delivering education to students in war-torn Yemen and built a text-message-based learning platform, then shifted Arist toward training employees at Fortune 500 companies, becoming one of OpenAI’s early partners along the way.

He started to notice a pattern: companies would pay consultants millions to diagnose a problem, then pay Arist a few hundred thousand dollars to train employees to fix it. In his experience, the consultants got the diagnosis wrong about 90% of the time.

That prompted Arist to move from training employees to diagnosing the problems companies were trying to solve. Ioffe pointed to a major software company whose data was merely pointing out what was happening instead of why.

Before AI can recommend something as consequential as a layoff, it first needs to understand what’s happening inside a company. Arist’s agents can decide whom to interview, ask questions, and weigh responses against information such as an employee’s tenure, performance, and past engagement scores. Ioffe said that helps the system distinguish the loudest complaints from problems affecting the wider organization. The agents will also push back, he said, if an executive frames a question to get the answer they want.

But gathering that information could raise concerns about how candid employees are willing to be with an AI agent working on behalf of their employer, especially when its findings could influence decisions about their jobs.
Ioffe argued that employees may actually be more candid with AI agents than with another person, making it easier for companies to uncover problems that might otherwise go unreported.
“Turns out that humans are not that good at listening,” he quipped.
Rather than replacing executives or consultants, Ioffe sees AI’s biggest opportunity in helping companies identify problems and act on them faster.
“If you can get to the truth much faster, then a 50,000-person enterprise can move at the speed of a 50-person startup,” Ioffe said.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/test-stor.title: AI Startup Raises Millions to Modernize Auto Retail
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/test-stor.author: Jane Doe
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence is transforming traditional car dealerships by automating complex customer workflows.
The startup connects directly to dealership dealer management software to handle appointments and trade-ins.
Investors led by major venture funds poured substantial capital into the company's expansion plans.
With hundreds of dealerships signed up, the platform continues to streamline service lane operations.
